<skill_content name="frontend-design">
# Skill: frontend-design

# Frontend Design

Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for giving every client a visual identity that could not be mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take one real aesthetic risk you can justify.

## Ground it in the subject

If the brief does not pin down what the product or subject is, pin it yourself before designing: name one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job, and state your choice. If there's any information in your memory about the human's preferences, context about what they're building, or designs you've made before – use that as a hint. The subject's own world, its materials, instruments, artifacts, and vernacular, is where distinctive choices come from. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.

## Design principles

For web designs, the hero is a thesis. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in whatever form makes sense for it: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the template answer, only use if that's truly the best option.

Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.

Structure is information. Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated.

Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.

Consider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.

## Process: brainstorm, explore, plan, critique, build, critique again

For calibration: AI-generated design right now clusters around three looks: (1) a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta accent; (2) a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent; (3) a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns. All three are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. Just like a human designer who's hired, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.

Work in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the human's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and signature. Color: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values. Type: the typefaces for 2+ roles (a characterful display face that's used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed). Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Signature: the single unique element this page will be remembered by that embodies the brief in an appropriate way.

Then review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief — revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan exactly and deriving every color and type decision from it.

When writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and a element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with paddings/margins between sections.

Try to do a lot of this planning and iteration in your thinking, and only show ideas to the user when you have higher confidence it'll delight them.

## Restraint and self-critique

Spend your boldness in one place. Let the signature element be the one memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Not taking a risk can be a risk itself! Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots if your environment supports it – a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creators have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.

## More on writing in design

Words appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand, and therefore easier to use. They are design material, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality to copy that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.

Write from the end user's side of the screen. Name things by what people control and recognize, never by how the system is built. A person manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific is always better than being clever.

Use active voice as default. A control should say exactly what happens when it's used: "Save changes," not "Submit." An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says "Publish" produces a toast that says "Published." The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.

Treat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. An empty screen is an invitation to act.

Keep the register conversational and tuned: plain verbs, sentence case, no filler, with tone matched to the brand and the audience. Let each element do exactly one job. A label labels, an example demonstrates, and nothing quietly does double duty.

Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the template answer, only use if that's truly the best option.

Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.

Structure is information. Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated.

Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.

Consider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.

## Process: brainstorm, explore, plan, critique, build, critique again

For calibration: AI-generated design right now clusters around three looks: (1) a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta accent; (2) a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent; (3) a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns. All three are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. Just like a human designer who's hired, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.

Work in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the human's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and signature. Color: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values. Type: the typefaces for 2+ roles (a characterful display face that's used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed). Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Signature: the single unique element this page will be remembered by that embodies the brief in an appropriate way.

Then review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief — revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan exactly and deriving every color and type decision from it.

When writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and a element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with paddings/margins between sections.

Try to do a lot of this planning and iteration in your thinking, and only show ideas to the user when you have higher confidence it'll delight them.

## Restraint and self-critique

Spend your boldness in one place. Let the signature element be the one memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Not taking a risk can be a risk itself! Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots if your environment supports it – a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creators have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.

## More on writing in design

Words appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand, and therefore easier to use. They are design material, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality to copy that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.

Write from the end user's side of the screen. Name things by what people control and recognize, never by how the system is built. A person manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific is always better than being clever.

Use active voice as default. A control should say exactly what happens when it's used: "Save changes," not "Submit." An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says "Publish" produces a toast that says "Published." The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.

Treat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. An empty screen is an invitation to act.

Keep the register conversational and tuned: plain verbs, sentence case, no filler, with tone matched to the brand and the audience. Let each element do exactly one job. A label labels, an example demonstrates, and nothing quietly does double duty.

20:  * The headline sentence is a working template: callers that pass
21:  * baseline metrics get the honest "at baseline" wording, and callers
22:  * that pass metrics already shocked by applyTwist pass the matching
23:  * scenario label, so the sentence can never claim a twist the numbers
24:  * did not run.
25:  *
26:  * Pure module: no React, no fetch, no artifact reads. The E5 view feeds
27:  * it the profiles the loader already parsed.
28:  */
29: 
30: /** One atlas row: a profile id plus the metrics the ladder reads. */
31: export interface AtlasEntry extends WeatherMetrics {
32:   account_id: string
33: }
34: 
35: /** Count or percent per state, keyed by the canonical state union. */
36: export type WeatherCounts = Record<WeatherState, number>
37: 
38: export interface StormAtlasSummary {
39:   /** Entries counted (the population under the caller's scenario). */
40:   total: number
41:   /** Accounts per weather state, integers. */
42:   counts: WeatherCounts
43:   /** Whole percent per state (rounding may drift a point across states). */
44:   percents: WeatherPercents
45:   /** The state the headline speaks about. */
46:   headlineState: WeatherState
47:   /** Accounts in that state. */
48:   headlineCount: number
49:   /** "1 in N" divisor over the whole population, null when the count is 0. */
50:   oneInN: number | null
51:   /** The working template sentence, ready to render. */
52:   headline: string
53:   /** What the numbers ran under, printed at the end of the headline. */
54:   scenarioLabel: string
55: }
56: 
57: export type WeatherPercents = Record<WeatherState, number>
58: 
59: export interface StormAtlasOptions {
60:   /** State the headline reports, default storm (the warning vocabulary). */
61:   headlineState?: WeatherState
62:   /** Scenario suffix, default honest baseline wording. */
63:   scenarioLabel?: string
64: }
65: 
66: /** Default headline state: the storm warning the pitch quotes. */
67: export const DEFAULT_HEADLINE_STATE: WeatherState = 'storm'
68: 
69: /** Default scenario wording: only a caller that ran a twist says otherwise. */
70: export const DEFAULT_SCENARIO_LABEL = 'at baseline'
71: 
72: /** All zero counts, in canonical key order. */
73: export function emptyCounts(): WeatherCounts {
74:   const counts = {} as WeatherCounts
75:   for (const state of WEATHER_STATES) {
76:     counts[state] = 0
77:   }
78:   return counts
79: }
80: 
81: function emptyPercents(): WeatherPercents {
82:   const percents = {} as WeatherPercents
83:   for (const state of WEATHER_STATES) {
84:     percents[state] = 0
85:   }
86:   return percents
87: }
88: 
89: /**
90:  * Count every entry's weather state once. Null, undefined, and empty
91:  * arrays aggregate to a zero summary with an honest placeholder
92:  * headline, so the atlas grid can mount before the loader resolves.
93:  */
94: export function summarizeStormAtlas(
95:   entries: readonly AtlasEntry[] | null | undefined,
96:   options: StormAtlasOptions = {},
97: ): StormAtlasSummary {
98:   const list = entries ?? []
99:   const headlineState = options.headlineState ?? DEFAULT_HEADLINE_STATE
100:   const scenarioLabel = options.scenarioLabel ?? DEFAULT_SCENARIO_LABEL
101: 
102:   const counts = emptyCounts()
103:   for (const entry of list) {
104:     if (!entry || typeof entry !== 'object') {
105:       continue
106:     }
107:     counts[weatherState(entry)] += 1
108:   }
109: 
110:   // Total is the sum of the counts, so a defensively skipped entry can
111:   // never inflate the population the percents divide by.
112:   let total = 0
113:   for (const state of WEATHER_STATES) {
114:     total += counts[state]
115:   }
116:   const percents = emptyPercents()
117:   if (total > 0) {
118:     for (const state of WEATHER_STATES) {
119:       percents[state] = roundHalfUp(counts[state] * 100, total)
120:     }
121:   }
122: 
123:   const headlineCount = counts[headlineState]
124:   const oneInN = headlineCount > 0 ? roundHalfUp(total, headlineCount) : null
125:   const headline = headlineSentence(total, headlineState, headlineCount, oneInN, scenarioLabel)
126: 
127:   return {
128:     total,
129:     counts,
130:     percents,
131:     headlineState,
132:     headlineCount,
133:     oneInN,
134:     headline,
135:     scenarioLabel,
136:   }
137: }
138: 
139: /**
140:  * The working headline template: "1 in N accounts hits storm warning
141:  * under the standard EI twist", with honest fallbacks for an empty
142:  * population and a state that never fires in the data.
143:  */
144: function headlineSentence(
145:   total: number,
146:   state: WeatherState,
147:   count: number,
148:   oneInN: number | null,
149:   scenarioLabel: string,
150: ): string {
151:   const label = WEATHER_META[state].label.toLowerCase()
152:   if (total === 0) {
153:     return 'No accounts in the atlas yet'
154:   }
155:   if (count === 0 || oneInN === null) {
156:     return `No accounts hit ${label} ${scenarioLabel}`
157:   }
158:   return `1 in ${oneInN} accounts hits ${label} ${scenarioLabel}`
159: }
160: 
161: /**
162:  * Drill down helper: the account ids behind one state's cell, in the
163:  * order the caller passed them. The atlas cell click hands its state
164:  * here, and the view decides what to render with the list (this module
165:  * never navigates).
166:  */
167: export function accountsInState(
168:   entries: readonly AtlasEntry[] | null | undefined,
169:   state: WeatherState,
170: ): readonly string[] {
171:   const list = entries ?? []
172:   return list
173:     .filter((entry) => entry && typeof entry === 'object' && weatherState(entry) === state)
174:     .map((entry) => entry.account_id)
175: }
176: 
177: /** Severity ordered state list for atlas grids and legends. */
178: export const ATLAS_ORDER: readonly WeatherState[] = SEVERITY_ORDER

8:  *

183:  * 2. runway_state no_shortfall reads clear before any threshold.

185:  *    flag also reads flood: the account is already underwater, and clear
186:  *    skies over a known negative buffer would be the dishonest render.
187:  * 4. runway 0.1 to 2.9 months reads storm.

190:  *    ratio against zero spending is undefined, and a zero income flag
191:  *    with no spending is a no shortfall account, not a drought).
192:  * 6. runway 3.0 to 11.9 reads rain when spending exceeds income, the
193:  *    spending driven band.
194:  * 7. runway 12.0 to 23.9 reads overcast, and 24.0 and up reads cloudy,
195:  *    both only while spending exceeds income.
196:  * 8. Everything else reads clear: no monthly shortfall, or a runway of
197:  *    12.0 months and up that no spending driven band claimed. This is
198:  *    what keeps all seven states reachable, since clear and overcast
199:  *    would otherwise both claim the 12 to 24 month window.
200:  *
201:  * thin_history, pensioner, and defaulted_loan deliberately do not change
202:  * the state: research assigns them chip modifiers (fog confidence chip,
203:  * eclipse modifier, hail warning on shock only) that the surfaces render
204:  * beside the state instead of replacing it.
205:  */
206: export function weatherState(metrics: WeatherMetrics): WeatherState {
207:   if (metrics.runway_state === 'buffer_depleted') {
208:     return 'flood'
209:   }
210:   if (metrics.runway_state === 'no_shortfall') {
211:     return 'clear'
212:   }
213: 
214:   const deci = deciMonthsOf(metrics)
215:   if (deci <= 0 || metrics.buffer_cents <= 0 || metrics.flags?.negative_buffer === true) {
216:     return 'flood'
217:   }
218:   if (deci < DECI_STORM_MAX + 1) {
219:     return 'storm'
220:   }
221: 
222:   const income = metrics.income_cents
223:   const spending = metrics.spending_cents
224:   // Integer form of income / spending <= 0.65, both operands cents, so
225:   // no float can sit on the drought boundary.
226:   if (spending > 0 && income * 100 <= spending * INCOME_RATIO_PCT) {
227:     return 'drought'
228:   }
229: 
230:   const gapAboveZero = metrics.gap_cents > 0
231:   if (deci < DECI_RAIN_MAX + 1) {
232:     return gapAboveZero ? 'rain' : 'clear'
233:   }
234:   if (deci < DECI_OVERCAST_MAX + 1) {
235:     return gapAboveZero ? 'overcast' : 'clear'
236:   }
237:   return gapAboveZero ? 'cloudy' : 'clear'
238: }
239: 
240: /**
241:  * Severity from 0 (calm) to 1 (underwater), the researched formula
242:  * clamp(1 minus runway months / 12, 0, 1) over the same integer tenths
243:  * the state ladder reads. It drives motion intensity and arc gauges
244:  * only: the division happens once, at the end, and the result is
245:  * display data that never decides a branch anywhere in the repo.
246:  */
247: export function weatherSeverity(metrics: WeatherMetrics): number {
248:   if (metrics.runway_state === 'buffer_depleted') {
249:     return 1
250:   }
251:   if (metrics.runway_state === 'no_shortfall') {
252:     return 0
253:   }
254:   const deci = Math.max(0, deciMonthsOf(metrics))
255:   const capped = Math.min(deci, SEVERITY_REFERENCE_DECI)
256:   return (SEVERITY_REFERENCE_DECI - capped) / SEVERITY_REFERENCE_DECI
257: }

179:  * order (first match wins):

For 'Furnace repair' → 'under the furnace repair twist'. For 'Laid off and bills up' → 'under the laid off and bills up twist'.

Wait, careful: 'Laid off'.toLowerCase() = 'laid off'. Good.

But matching presets: a preset's twist must be normalized before comparison (normalizeTwist(preset.twist)) — note the consoleStore matchPreset does exactly that. So in shockedAtlasScenario: for each preset in SHOCK_PRESETS, if sameTwist(normalizeTwist(preset.twist), twist) → label. Note twist passed in might not be normalized... The store always keeps twist normalized. But for safety, compare normalizeTwist(twist) against normalizeTwist(preset.twist).

Hmm — one subtlety: normalizeTwist(preset.twist) for layoff = {jobLoss:true, incomeFactor:0.55, billsDeltaPct:0, oneOffMonthsTenths:0, extraMonthlyCents:0, durationMonths:6}. Good, I understand the cp design tokens. There's a `data-band` attribute pattern for band colors: `.cp-verdict[data-band='critical'] { --cp-band: var(--cp-band-critical); }` etc.

So in atlas.css, I can do the same: `.ax-plot[data-band='...']` or set `--ax-band` per element via data-band attributes. For SVG fills, I can use `fill="var(--cp-band-storm)"`? In SVG, CSS custom properties work in fill via style attribute or CSS. React: `<circle style={{ fill: ... }}>`. Or use a class with fill set in CSS: `.ax-dot[data-band='storm_warning'] { fill: var(--cp-band-storm); }`. That's cleaner: attribute-based CSS, React just sets data-band.

But the spec says "4,500 memoized circles keyed by account_id (r 2.6, band fill var(--cp-band-*) at 0.75 opacity)". So fill uses var(--cp-band-*). I can set `fill` via CSS class per data-band, or inline style with the var. Inline style: `style={{ fill: `var(--cp-band-${suffix})`, opacity: 0.75 }}`? Hmm — "at 0.75 opacity". Could be fill-opacity.

Careful about performance: 4,500 circles with inline styles is fine.

Actually the design mentions "attribute-only dot updates" for perf: meaning when twist changes, dots update attributes only (React re-renders 4,500 circles but with memoized array). Hmm, "4,500 memoized circles keyed by account_id" — memoized meaning the dots array is memoized in useMemo (buildAtlasPlot in AtlasSection's one useMemo).

Wait: "Perf: 4,500 applyTwist ~2-5 ms per twist change inside the one useMemo; attribute-only dot updates." Since React19 renders SVG circles from the array, updates are attribute updates (no DOM node replacement because keys are stable). Fine.

Read file /Users/ajeet/Projects/Hackathons/Sheridan Datathon 2026/docs/architecture.md, lines 55-174
55: ## Stack
56: 
57: - Python 3.14 + uv + pandas + numpy for the offline engine pipeline;
58:   pytest for tests. Modules are header-style, snake_case, type hinted.
59: - React 19, Vite 6, TypeScript 5.7 strict, Tailwind 3.4, Zustand 5,
60:   Vitest for the site.
61: - three 0.170 + @react-three/fiber is legacy from the dropped game
62:   layer (PlayView); not part of the engine surface.
63: - GitHub Pages via GitHub Actions, base path aware.
64: - Entire for graph queries, checkpoints, and the build trail.
65: 
66: ## Phases E1 to E7
67: 
68: - **E1 profile precompute (COMPLETE).** scripts/engine loads checksum
69:   verified CSVs, computes the judge metrics in integer cents, and
70:   writes public/data/engine/profiles.json (meta plus one profile per
71:   account). Shipped and verified Nov 07 2026.
72: - **E2 console base.** Account lookup over 4500 ids, baseline card,
73:   shock presets plus sliders, verdict, and plan text.
74: - **E3 weather viz.** Forecast strip, storm front, landfall pin,
75:   verdict bands, and the EI-cliff overlay.
76: - **E4 plan engine.** Goal math plus backup levers with +N months
77:   effects.
78: - **E5 Storm Atlas.** Population headline plus strip-plot drill-down.
79: - **E6 judge mode.** Keyboard shortcuts, edge-account guards,
80:   rehearsal, and paper fallback.
81: - **E7 Solana A+ touch.** Gated memo package plus honest receipt badge
82:   in the verdict card.
83: 
84: ### Considered enhancements (secondary)
85: 
86: - **Natural language shock input via the Gemini API.** User provided
87:   idea, secondary to the approved phase list above, and not yet
88:   scheduled. A judge or user types a phrase like "laid off and rent up
89:   15%" and it maps to the twist fields incomeFactor, billsDeltaPct,
90:   and oneOffMonthsOfSpend instead of clicking preset buttons. Risks:
91:   live API dependency at the booth (network is allowed but must never
92:   be required, so it must degrade gracefully to the preset buttons);
93:   parsing must be validated against the twist schema before applying;
94:   and it belongs after E2 where the shock presets exist.
95: 
96: ## Data layer
97: 
98: ```
99: data/tangerine/*.csv (checksums in SHA256SUMS)
100:     -> scripts/engine/load.py      (verify, integer cent parse, grouping)
101:     -> scripts/engine/metrics.py   (pure I, F, S, B, H, gap, flags)
102:     -> scripts/engine/shocks.py    (pure runway function)
103:     -> scripts/engine/build.py     (meta + profiles, deterministic)
104:     -> public/data/engine/profiles.json
105:     -> scripts/engine/verify.py    (naive csv recompute, drift diff, SHA256)
106: ```
107: 
108: - Sources: monthly_summary.csv (185,326 rows), loans.csv (682),
109:   accounts.csv (4,500), over 2020-01 to 2025-12.
110: - The artifact: about 4.7 MB compact JSON, 4500 profiles, meta block
111:   with sources, definitions, checksum recipe, and edge flag counts
112:   (pensioner 740, thin_history 377, zero_income 14, defaulted_loan 45,
113:   negative_buffer 23 in the shipped build).
114: - Loan cross check in the build report: 448 loans running by the status
115:   rule (C or D), 448 running by schedule (end month past 2025-12), 0
116:   disagreements.
117: - Provenance: each profile carries a check_sum over
118:   `account_id:month` rows and `money_in` cents, recipe in
119:   pipeline_lib.checksum and mirrored by src/data/checksum.ts.
120: - Existing site data (world.json, transactions.json, findings.json,
121:   model_card.json) is unchanged; the engine adds public/data/engine/.
122: 
123: ## Verification
124: 
125: - `uv run python -m scripts.engine.build`: checksum gate, build report
126:   with source sha256 prefixes, edge flag counts (all five must be
127:   nonzero), loan cross check, artifact size, PASS line.
128: - `uv run python -m scripts.engine.verify`: independent naive csv
129:   recomputation of all 4500 accounts with no pandas, no numpy, and no
130:   import of scripts.engine.metrics; exact field by field diff; dash
131:   violation scan over every artifact string; prints the artifact SHA256;
132:   exits non zero on any drift.
133: - `uv run pytest -q`: golden fixtures asserted against both
134:   metrics.pipeline and the shipped artifact entry (five real accounts
135:   covering odd and even medians, the half cent tie, thin history with
136:   zero income, a running loan, a defaulted loan, and every runway
137:   branch), schema validation, check_sum recomputation for all accounts,
138:   determinism (two consecutive builds byte identical and equal to the
139:   shipped file).
140: - `scripts/engine/test_metrics.py`: rounding ties, every runway branch
141:   including buffer_depleted, no_shortfall, cap and deci half ties, thin
142:   history buffer, flag thresholds.
143: - Rule drift guard: contract strings in verify.py are duplicated from
144:   build.py on purpose, so a silent edit to a definition fails
145:   verification.
146: 
147: ## Frontend layering
148: 
149: 1. **Data (src/data):** typed loaders with schema validation
150:    (profiles loader lands in E2), checksum mirror, resolveRows for
151:    provenance. No math, no React.
152: 2. **Core (src/lib):** pure functions only. The E2 shock math and E4
153:    plan math live here as TypeScript twins of the Python rules; they
154:    must never import React and must operate on integer cents.
155: 3. **Views (src/components):** engine console view (E2), weather
156:    forecast views (E3), Storm Atlas (E5). Views render numbers from
157:    loaders and core functions; inline money math in a component is a
158:    review failure. Old report and game views are dropped as surfaces.
159: 4. **Render (src/components/river, scene):** presentation only, swappable
160:    without touching layers 1 to 3.
161: 
162: Load once, memoize: profiles.json is fetched a single time and parsed
163: once per session (the same pattern as loadSharedFindingsReport).
164: 
165: ## Performance budget
166: 
167: - Artifact: keep profiles.json under 5 MB and a single request; parse
168:   once, index 4500 account ids for search under 10 ms.
169: - Shock recalculation: integer arithmetic, under 1 ms per interaction,
170:   no async hop for a slider move.
171: - Existing game budget unchanged: 60 fps on integrated GPU, dpr capped
172:   at 1.5, no shadow maps, Html labels capped near 20 with distance
173:   culling.
174: - Everything bundled for offline booths; no runtime network calls

function fnv1a(text: string): number {

export function shockedAtlasScenario(
  profiles: readonly AccountProfile[] | null | undefined,
  twist: Twist,
): AtlasScenario {
  const list = profiles ?? []
  const entries: AtlasEntry[] = new Array(list.length)
  for (let i = 0; i < list.length; i++) {
    const profile = list[i]
    const result = applyTwist(profile, twist)
    entries[i] = { account_id: profile.account_id, runway_state: result.runway.state, runway_deci_months: result.runway.deciMonths }
  }
  return { entries, scenarioLabel: atlasScenarioLabel(twist) }
}

```ts
function fnv1a(text: string): number {
  let hash = 0x811c9dc5
  for (let i = 0; i < text.length; i++) {
    hash ^= text.charCodeAt(i)
    hash = Math.imul(hash, 0x01000193)
  }
  return hash >>> 0
}
function hash01(text: string): number {
  return fnv1a(text) / 0x1_0000_0000
}
export function jitterFor(accountId: string): number {
  return hash01(accountId)
}
```

```ts
function fnv1a(text: string): number {
  let hash = 0x811c9dc5
  for (let i = 0; i < text.length; i++) {
    hash ^= text.charCodeAt(i)
    hash = Math.imul(hash, 0x01000193)
  }
  return hash >>> 0
}
function hash01(text: string): number {
  return fnv1a(text) / 0x1_0000_0000
}
export function jitterFor(accountId: string): number {
  return hash01(accountId)
}

```ts
function fnv1a(text: string): number {
  let hash = 0x811c9dc5
  for (let i = 0; i < text.length; i++) {
    hash ^= text.charCodeAt(i)
    hash = Math.imul(hash, 0x01000193)
  }
  return hash >>> 0
}
function hash01(text: string): number {
  return fnv1a(text) / 0x1_0000_0000
}
export function jitterFor(accountId: string): number {
  return hash01(accountId)

content.text:
Good — I now understand the conventions well. Note: ForecastStrip uses `band.tailwind` classes for color (`text-cp-*`) with `currentColor` in CSS (wx-slot uses currentColor presumably).

Let me check weather.css .wx-slot rule to see how fill works with the tailwind class.

Also, I should now decide: for the strip plot dots, use `className={`ax-dot ${band.tailwind}`}` with CSS `fill: currentColor`? The spec says "band fill var(--cp-band-*) at 0.75 opacity". So use `var(--cp-band-*)` directly. Mapping band id → CSS var suffix: critical→critical, storm_warning→storm, watch→watch, fair_skies→fair, clear→clear.

I'll define in atlas.css:
```css
.ax-dot { fill: var(--cp-ink-faint); opacity: 0.75; }
.ax-dot[data-band='critical'] { fill: var(--cp-band-critical); }
...
```
And background segments:
```css
.ax-seg[data-band='critical'] { fill: var(--cp-band-critical); opacity: 0.10; }
```

That satisfies "band fill var(--cp-band-*) at 0.75 opacity" (the dot fill resolves to var(--cp-band-*), opacity 0.75).

Hmm — the spec literally says circles have `fill var(--cp-band-*)` — CSS class with data-band achieves exactly that. Alternatively inline style `style={{fill: 'var(--cp-band-critical)'}}`. CSS classes are cleaner and allow a single opacity rule.

But wait: will the test be able to verify band fill? Test can check `data-band` attribute on circles. Good.

Now the silhouette bars: `.ax-bar[data-band=...]` fill band color at low opacity.

Ticks: `<text>` elements with class `ax-tick`.

Now, let me think about `role="img"` + `aria-label`: also `focusable`? Dots are clickable → they should be keyboard accessible? 4500 focusable circles would be a keyboard nightmare. Better: dots are click targets via mouse, but keyboard users use... hmm. Accessibility: The design says "dot click -> onSelectAccount(id)". For a11y, making4500 SVG circles focusable is bad practice. 

Options: keep circles as `<circle>` with onClick and `role="button"`? That'd be 4500 tab stops. Not good.

Better approach: make the plot `role="img"` (non-interactive to AT), and provide an accessible fallback: the AccountLookup already exists in ConsoleView for keyboard users (typed id search). The caption can say: "Every dot is one account... Select an account by its id in the console lookup." Hmm, but then dot clicks are mouse-only.

The design explicitly says role="img" + aria-label. role="img" makes children presentational (AT ignores inner content), so click handlers on circles inside role="img" are effectively mouse-only. That's the approved design; the keyboard path is the existing lookup. I'll note in the report that keyboard users reach accounts through the existing lookup (documented in caption? maybe not).

Hmm, should I add `aria-hidden` to interactive circles? role="img" already hides descendants. Fine.

Visible keyboard focus: my checklist item — the section's interactive elements: cells are divs (not interactive), dots mouse-only. Focus indicators exist on existing controls. I'll ensure any real buttons I add have focus-visible styles. If StormAtlas cells aren't buttons (no callback), no focus needed. I'll keep cells as static divs (no drill-down callback in the new props).

Wait — but then what about drill-down? "drill-down uses the EXISTING selectAccount action only" — drill-down happens via dot click in the strip plot (selectAccount + scroll to console). The band cells are informational. OK.

Now, mobile/responsive: svg width 100% with viewBox — scales down. Cells use auto-fit grid. Headline uses clamp(). Touch targets: dots are small (r2.6) — hit area concern on mobile, but there's the lookup for that. I could add a larger transparent hit radius? Not in spec. Skip.

Now — one important perf consideration: 4,500 circles with per-circle onClick in React. React attaches listeners at root (event delegation), so it's fine.

Rendering4,500 circles in jsdom for app.smoke: let's estimate. React19 createRoot + jsdom: creating 4500 SVG elements... could be ~500ms-1.5s. The app smoke test does this twice (two tests boot the shell) + the AtlasSection smoke test. Total maybe +2-4s. Acceptable (baseline1.1s total... it would triple). Hmm, it's fine as long as tests pass.

Actually wait — there's a subtlety: in app.smoke.test.ts, `until(container, 'Know the customer')` polls textContent every 5ms — with heavy synchronous renders, fine.

Let me also think about `renderToString` in the server-render test: rendering App with idle state → AtlasSection renders loading (no dots). Good.

Now — does AtlasSection need `boot()`? ConsoleView already boots. AtlasSection reads bundle/status. If AtlasSection is mounted and ConsoleView also mounts, both call... ConsoleView has `useEffect(() => void boot(), [boot])`. AtlasSection shouldn't call boot (boot is idempotent anyway). Design says reads useConsole (bundle, status, twist, selectAccount) — no boot. OK.

Now let me write the code. Stage 1 first.

/**
 * Clamp one runway reading to the artifact range the E1 loader
 * enforces (0 to 1200 tenths). A non finite reading reads 0, which
 * lands on Critical: unknown data must never render as clear skies.

export function clampDeciMonths(raw: number): number {

  }
  return Math.min(RUNWAY_CAP_DECI_MONTHS, Math.max(0, raw))

/**
 * Clamp one runway reading to the artifact range the E1 loader
 * enforces (0 to 1200 tenths). A non finite reading reads 0, which
 * lands on Critical: unknown data must never render as clear skies.
 */
export function clampDeciMonths(raw: number): number {
  if (!Number.isFinite(raw)) {
    return 0
  }
  return Math.min(RUNWAY_CAP_DECI_MONTHS, Math.max(0, raw))
}
```

  return verdictBand({
    state: entry.runway_state,
    deciMonths: clampDeciMonths(entry.runway_deci_months),
  }).id
}

/**
 * FNV-1a over UTF-16 code units, returned as a unit fraction in
 * [0, 1). Deterministic across runs and platforms, which is what lets
 * a dot keep its place between renders and lets the golden test pin
 * one exact value.
 */
function hash01(text: string): number {
  let hash = 0x811c9dc5
  for (let index = 0; index < text.length; index += 1) {
    hash ^= text.charCodeAt(index)
    hash = Math.imul(hash, 0x01000193)
  }
  return (hash >>> 0) / 0x100000000
}

export function jitterFor(accountId: string): number {
  return hash01(accountId)
}

export function buildAtlasPlot(entries: readonly AtlasEntry[] | null | undefined): AtlasPlot {
  const list = entries ?? []
  const bins: AtlasBin[] = ATLAS_BIN_SPECS.map((spec) => ({
    label: spec.label,
    loDeci: spec.loDeci,
    hiDeci: spec.hiDeci,
    overflow: spec.overflow,
    count: 0,
    countsByBand: emptyBandCounts(),
  }))
  const dots: AtlasDot[] = []
  for (const entry of list) {
    if (!entry || typeof entry !== 'object') continue
    const deciMonths = clampDeciMonths(entry.runway_deci_months)
    const band = entryBand(entry)
    const binIndex = binIndexFor(deciMonths)
    const bin = bins[binIndex]
    if (!bin) continue
    bin.count += 1
    bin.countsByBand[band] += 1
    const localT = bin.overflow
      ? jitterFor(entry.account_id)
      : (deciMonths - bin.loDeci) / (bin.hiDeci - bin.loDeci)
    dots.push({
      account_id: entry.account_id,
      band,
      deciMonths,
      x: ATLAS_PAD_X + ((binIndex + localT) / ATLAS_BIN_COUNT) * ATLAS_PLOT_W,
      y: ATLAS_DOT_TOP + hash01(`${entry.account_id}:y`) * ATLAS_DOT_H,
    })
  }
  const capBin = bins[ATLAS_BIN_COUNT - 1] ?? ...
  return { dots, bins, total: dots.length, capBin }
}

/**
 * FNV-1a over UTF-16 code units, returned as a unit fraction in
 * [0, 1). Deterministic across runs and platforms, which is what lets
 * a dot keep its place between renders and lets the golden test pin
 * one exact value.
 */
function hash01(text: string): number {
  let hash = 0x811c9dc5
  for (let index = 0; index < text.length; index += 1) {
    hash ^= text.charCodeAt(index)
    hash = Math.imul(hash, 0x01000193)
  }
  return (hash >>> 0) / 0x100000000
}

content.text:
index.css is imported in main.tsx (global) ✓. Fonts: display = mono stack, body = system-ui. So the design system is mono display + sans body. For the atlas headline (the pitch read), using the mono display at a large size fits the instrument aesthetic. To make the headline distinctive, I could make the PERCENT a separate span in band color (the storm color) — the headline number pops. That's a nice signature touch: `61%` in --cp-band-storm (amber) while the rest is paper. But the headline comes as one string from the lib. To color the percent, I'd have to split the string in the component (string surgery — brittle, and honesty rule says wording comes from the lib). Alternative: render headline as-is (one h2), and let the design carry weight through size/position instead. Hmm, splitting `${percent}% of accounts...` — I could render `

{summary.headline}

` plainly. Simpler and honest. The signature element of this section = the strip plot (the 4,500 dot field). Keep the headline typographically strong but plain. Actually, I can do something honest and non-brittle: put a large typographic treatment on the headline with a left border in storm color? Or an eyebrow above: "POPULATION, ALL 4,500 ACCOUNTS" (cp-eyebrow) then the h2 headline. That matches the panel pattern (cp-eyebrow + cp-title). But cp-eyebrow is teal uppercase; for atlas I'll make an ax-eyebrow. Design plan for the section: ``` +--------------------------------------------------------------+ | POPULATION, 4,500 ACCOUNTS (eyebrow) | | 10% of accounts would have under 3 months of runway ... <- headline (large)| | 435 of 4,500 accounts · At baseline: 1% (60 of 4,500) <- subline | | [⛈ Critical] [🌧 Storm warning] [☁ Watch] [⛅ Fair] [☀ Clear] <- cells | | [ strip plot: tinted segments, silhouette, 4,500 dots ] | | Every dot is one account. Axis segments follow... (caption) | +--------------------------------------------------------------+ ``` Wait: should the eyebrow be part of StormAtlas? The design says StormAtlas renders headline + subline + 5 cells. The eyebrow is extra. I'll skip the eyebrow to stay close to spec... Actually a section needs some identification for screen readers. The h2 IS the heading (sentence). Fine, no eyebrow. Hmm, but a heading that reads "10% of accounts would have under 3 months of runway under the laid off twist" is a decent h2. Actually, for a11y the aria-label of the plot carries the headline too. Let me keep it minimal per spec: h2 headline, subline, cells. Now — one more consideration on responsive: cells grid auto-fit minmax(9.5rem,1fr) → on a 320px screen: 9.5rem = 152px → 1 column? 320-2*16(padding)-2*24(panel padding) =240 → 1 column of 152+... auto-fit would give 1 column. Fine, touch-friendly. Strip plot on mobile: svg scales to width; at 320px wide, the 840-unit axis → dots become sub-pixel (r2.6 *320/960 = 0.87px). Dots will be tiny but still a texture. Ticks at font 11 → ~3.7px text — unreadable on mobile. Hmm. Responsive concern: the caption explains, but tick text tiny. Options: increase font-size in viewBox units for ticks (e.g., 16 units → 5.3px at 320px). Still small. Real fix: min-width with horizontal scroll on small screens? Or accept it (the console's other surfaces have similar issues? ForecastStrip uses 720 viewBox with month labels ~11 units → at 360px width, ~5.5px). So the existing E3 strip has the same characteristic. Consistency: accept, but bump tick font to 14 units for legibility (at desktop 960px wide → 14px ✓; at 360px → 5px✗). Alternative: allow the figure to scroll horizontally on narrow screens: `.ax-figure { overflow-x: auto } .ax-plot { min-width: 560px }`? That gives a horizontal scrollbar on mobile — a common pattern for dense plots, keeps ticks legible (560/960 * 14 = 8.2px, meh). Given the booth/judge context is a desktop demo, and the checklist wants responsive down to mobile, I'll do: svg width 100%, no scroll; tick font-size 15 units (at 960 → 15px desktop; at 360 → 5.6px mobile, small but the caption carries meaning). Hmm. Better: make the tick labels HTML? No, they're inside the svg per spec ("ticks ... " within the svg presumably). Let me reconsider: on mobile the whole app is a dense dashboard (cp panels with tables). The E3 strip already renders720-unit viewBox text at small sizes. I'll match: font-size 14-15 units for ticks. And I'll note it in the report. Actually, a cleaner responsive move: give the figure `overflow-x: auto` with `min-width: 480px` on the svg under a media query for ≤640px. Then at 360px viewport, the user scrolls the plot horizontally and text is 14 * (480/960) = 7px... still small. OK: set svg min-width 640px on small screens (scrollable): ticks14 * (640/960) = 9.3px at scroll position... acceptable-ish. And dots r2.6*(640/960)=1.7px. Honestly, for a datathon booth judged on a laptop, I'll go with width100%, no overflow scroll, tick font 15, and document. Simpler = better; horizontal scroll inside a page section can trap users. Hmm, but "Responsive down to mobile" is in my checklist. The layout (grid cells, headline clamp, svg scaling) IS responsive. Text legibility at 360px is the only compromise, shared with E3. I'll add a media query: below 40rem, increase tick font-size to 20 units (→7.5px at 320px)... that's still small but better; and increase unit note too. Eh — actually, let me reconsider: font-size 20 units at 960-wide desktop would be too big (20px). So a media query switching15 → 20 for narrow screens is right (20 *320/960 = 6.7px... ugh, because the whole viewBox scales down). The real problem: viewBox scaling shrinks everything proportionally. To keep text legible on mobile you must NOT scale the svg — i.e., fixed height with preserveAspectRatio... complexity not worth it. Decision: svg scales, ticks at 15 units, caption below in HTML (full size, readable), and the aria-label carries the headline. Mobile users read the headline + cells + caption (all HTML, full size) and see the dot texture. That's a defensible responsive story: the plot is decorative-supporting (role=img with aria-label), the numbers are HTML. Document in report. {summary.headline}

{`${figure(summary.headlineCount)} of ${total} accounts`} {baselineSummary ? ( {`At baseline: ${baselineSummary.headlinePercent}% (${figure(baselineSummary.headlineCount)} of ${figure(baselineSummary.total)})`} ) : null} {selectedId ? {`Tracking account ${selectedId}`} : null}

    {ATLAS_BAND_ORDER.map((bandId) => { const band = verdictBandById(bandId) const count = summary.counts[bandId] const percent = summary.percents[bandId] return (
  • {band.glyph} {band.label} {figure(count)} {`${percent}% of ${total}`}
    • ) })}
) } ``` Hmm — for a11y, the cells list should convey meaning: `
    ` with `
  • ` text content reads fine. Also maybe add `title={band.threshold}`? The spec doesn't ask. Could add threshold as a hidden span for screen readers? Baseline population: {critical:10, storm_warning:24, watch:5, fair_skies:6, clear:55} → total 100, headline 34 ✓. Twisted population: {critical:20, storm_warning:41, watch:10, fair_skies:9, clear:20} → total 100, headline 61 ✓. 'prints the baseline headline word for word': html contains '

    34% of accounts have under 3 months of runway at baseline

    '. React SSR renders className as `class`. ✓ 2. 'prints the twisted headline and the baseline comparison': with both props → contains '61% of accounts would have under 3 months of runway under the laid off twist' and 'At baseline: 34% (34 of 100)'. 3. 'shows the comparison subline only when a baseline arrives': without baselineSummary → not.toContain('At baseline:'); and subline contains '61 of 100 accounts'. 4. 'renders five band cells with glyph, label, count, percent': count `data-band="` occurrences = 5; each band label + glyph + count + percent present; order critical first, clear last (indexOf). 5. 'tracks the selected account': selectedId '68257' → contains 'Tracking account 68257'; without → not. 6. empty summary: summarizeStormAtlas([]) → headline 'No accounts in the atlas yet' and cells all 0 → contains '>0' five times? percent '0% of 0'. Assert `html.split('data-band="').length - 1 === 5` and contains 'No accounts in the atlas yet'. Let me count: for percent text '0% of 0' appears 5 times. Now write both files. One question: does the h2 wrap the headline with class ax-headline — in React 19 SSR, `className` → `class` ✓. Also: does renderToString escape '%'? No. Careful: the headline contains "10%" etc. Fine. Let me write the component.

import AtlasSection from './components/atlas/AtlasSection'
import ConsoleView from './components/console/ConsoleView'

/**
 * App shell (Phase E2, docs/decisions.md): the engine console is the
 * only mounted surface. The header names the instrument, the main slot
 * mounts the Storm Atlas section above the console (E5: the population
 * headline and strip plot, then the account cards it drills into),
 * and the footer cites the pipeline that wrote the bundled artifact.
 * The old findings report and game views stay in the tree as files but
 * are not mounted here; their own tests keep them honest until the

All gates green. Final report:

## QUESTIONS FOR USER
- Q1: `capBin` semantics were not defined in the design. I shipped it as the overflow `AtlasBin` object (`bins[5]`, `.overflow === true`), so the view can read `plot.capBin.count` without indexing. Confirm, or say if it should be a count.
- Q2: The design's example headline numbers (34% baseline, 61% under laid off) do not exist in the shipped artifact under the specified bands. With `DEFAULT_HEADLINE_BANDS = ['critical','storm_warning']` the real values are 1% baseline (60 of 4,500) and 10% under laid off (435 of 4,500). I implemented the specified sentence spec and bands, and pinned the real numbers in tests. Confirm the threshold is still "under 3 months", or name the band set that produces the intended headline.
- Q3: `StormAtlas` receives `selectedId` but the design never says what it renders. I ship a small "Tracking account N" chip in the subline row (the band cell cannot be marked without the entries). Confirm or specify.

## Frontend Implementation: Phase E5 Storm Atlas

### Design Plan
- **Palette** (existing console tokens, one source): `#ff6a4d` cp-critical, `#f4b740` cp-storm, `#8b7cf6` cp-watch, `#39c2e0` cp-fair, `#35d0ae` cp-clear, ground `#070c18` with `#e9effa` paper ink.
- **Typography**: display `ui-monospace` stack (headline, counts, tabular numerals), body `system-ui` (caption, notes), utility mono uppercase with 0.1em tracking (labels, ticks).
- **Layout**: one panel (`ax-shell`) holding headline, subline, five band cells (auto-fit grid, 44px min), then a full width `960x240` SVG strip plot with a hanging histogram silhouette, tinted segment columns, dot field, axis and month ticks.
- **ASCII wireframe**:
```
+----------------------------------------------------------+
| 10% of accounts would have under 3 months of runway ...  |  headline (largest type)
| 435 of 4,500 accounts   At baseline: 1% (60 of 4,500)   |  subline
| [⛈ Critical][🌧 Storm][☁ Watch][⛅ Fair][☀ Clear]        |  redundant encoding cells
| [tinted segments + silhouette bars + 4,500 dots]         |  signature strip plot
| 0  1  3  6  12  120  120+  (months)                     |
| Every dot is one account. Axis segments follow ...       |  caption
+----------------------------------------------------------+
```
- **Signature element**: the 4,500 dot strip plot on a piecewise axis (each sixth of the width is one band edge, so the under-3-month window is 1/6 of the picture, not a sliver), tinted by the same `--cp-band` tokens the console badge uses.

### Staged implementation (each stage written and verified green before the next)

| Stage | Files | Targeted result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 Fold | deleted `src/lib/weatherState.ts` (257 lines), `src/lib/weatherState.test.ts` (351 lines) | exactly 2 files red: `src/lib/stormAtlas.test.ts`, `src/components/atlas/StormAtlas.test.ts`; 426 tests passed elsewhere |
| 2 stormAtlas | `src/lib/stormAtlas.ts` rewrite, `src/lib/stormAtlas.test.ts` rewrite | 18 passed |
| 3 atlasPlot | `src/lib/atlasPlot.ts` new, `src/lib/atlasPlot.test.ts` new | 13 passed (14 after the segment tint assertion added in stage 5) |
| 4 StormAtlas | `src/components/atlas/StormAtlas.tsx` rewrite, `StormAtlas.test.ts` rewrite | 6 passed |
| 5 strip plot | `src/components/atlas/AtlasStripPlot.tsx` new, `AtlasStripPlot.test.ts` new, plus `ATLAS_BIN_BANDS` export in `atlasPlot.ts` | 7 passed |
| 6 section + css | `src/components/atlas/AtlasSection.tsx` new, `AtlasSection.test.ts` new, `src/components/atlas/atlas.css` new, `weather.css` wx-atlas block removed (lines 399 to 514), `import './atlas.css'` added to all three atlas components | 8 passed |
| 7 App mount | `src/App.tsx` (`<section id="atlas">` above `<div id="console">`, flex gap on main) | `app.smoke.test.ts` passed unchanged, 3 tests |
| 8 scan + gates | `src/dashScan.test.ts` (registered `stormAtlas.ts/.test`, `atlasPlot.ts/.test`, AUTO_DIRS `src/components/atlas`, CSS_FILES `atlas.css`, coverage assertions, E5 wording) | 3 passed, then full gates below |

### Fold confirmation
```
grep -rn "weatherState" src/
  src/components/weather/WeatherBands.test.ts:13   (comment, allowed)
  src/components/weather/WeatherBands.test.ts:84   (the source guard, allowed)
  src/lib/stormAtlas.ts:22                         (comment saying it is deleted)
  src/lib/forecast.ts:34                           (pre-existing comment; forecast* is do-not-touch)
```
No imports remain. `grep -rn "wx-atlas" src/` returns nothing. The negative buffer to flood and drought ratio branches went with the deleted file; `verdictBand` is the only ladder.

### Conservation and honesty results
- `stormAtlas.test.ts`: 5 band fixture (2/2/2/2/2 of 10), percents 20 each, thirds fixture proves percents may sum to 99, exact sentences for empty (`No accounts in the atlas yet`), zero count, baseline verb `have`, scenario verb `would have`, `At baseline` subline source, `accountsInBand` in caller order.
- Honesty: `shockedAtlasScenario(IDLE)` entries deep equal the recorded baseline for all 4,500 rows (0 mismatches); every preset twist yields `under the <label lowercase> twist` AND at least one row that differs from baseline (layoff 4,231 rows, cost spike 1,212, repair 1,080, combo 4,282); unmatched twists read `under the custom twist`; the layoff headline is asserted equal to its own computed percent plus the label, with `headlineCount > baseline`.
- `atlasPlot.test.ts`: golden `jitterFor('68257') = 2756683695 / 4294967296` (= 0.6418404390569776), boundary table 9/10/29/30/59/60/119/120/1199/1200 to bins 0..5, cap bin collects `finite 1200` and `no_shortfall 1200` (2 dots, spread apart, inside segment six), clamping of -50, 5000, NaN, Infinity, shipped artifact: 4,500 dots, every id exactly once, bin sums 4,500, `countsByBand` sums equal each bin count, dot band totals identical to `summarizeStormAtlas` counts.
- `AtlasSection.test.ts`: baseline `1% ... at baseline` with `60 of 4,500`, 4,500 circles, storm dots 26; after `applyPreset('layoff')` the field re colors (storm dots 26 to 384, critical 34 to 51) with `10% ... would have ... under the laid off twist`, `435 of 4,500`, `At baseline: 1% (60 of 4,500)`.

### Gate outputs
```
npx vitest run                      Test Files 44 passed (44)   Tests 479 passed (479)
npm run typecheck                   tsc --noEmit  (clean)
npm run build                       tsc build + vite build, 63 modules, dist assets written
uv run pytest -q                    160 passed in 3.78s
uv run python -m scripts.engine.verify
  artifact sha256 9ec428bf...   drift: none   scripts.engine.verify: PASS
```
466 baseline tests plus the new atlas tests, minus the 17 tests that lived in the two deleted weatherState files, all green.

### consoleStore zero-diff proof
```
git diff --stat src/state/consoleStore.ts     (empty)
git status --porcelain  ->  no src/state entry at all
```
Drill down goes through the existing `selectAccount` action only; `AtlasSection.test.ts` also greps `consoleStore.ts` for `atlas` and `Atlas` (both absent) and checks 14 E2 to E4 sources for atlas imports.

### Perf note
Measured on this machine with a temporary bench (deleted after): one twist change over 4,500 profiles runs `shockedAtlasScenario` in 0.53 ms and `summarize` (twisted) + `shockedAtlasScenario(IDLE)` + `summarize` (baseline) + `buildAtlasPlot` in 1.37 ms, 1.90 ms total, warm. The design's 2 to 5 ms estimate holds. Frame time for reconciling 4,500 keyed circles could not be measured: this checkout has no browser automation, so no 8x throttle drag frame was captured. The single path per band fallback is therefore NOT applied and is documented in the `AtlasStripPlot` header comment with the 50 ms trigger and the measurement gap stated honestly.

### Deviations and notes
1. `capBin`, `selectedId` rendering, and the example percentages are flagged in the questions above; all three are shipped best-effort and green.
2. `import './atlas.css'` was deferred from stages 4 and 5 to stage 6 (the stylesheet did not exist yet, and a missing CSS import fails module resolution in vitest), then added to all three components in stage 6 as the stage list assigns.
3. Keyboard access to a dot: the plot is `role="img"` per the design, so dots are mouse targets; the console lookup is the keyboard path and the component comment says so.
4. Mobile: the SVG scales with the viewport, so tick text shrinks below legibility on very narrow screens (same characteristic as the E3 forecast strip); headline, cells, subline, and caption are HTML and stay full size.
5. Untouched but noticed: `src/lib/forecast.ts` line 34 still says weatherState is "quarantined (E5 rework pending)", which is now stale. `forecast*` is do-not-touch, so it needs an orchestrator decision.
6. `README.md` and `docs/decisions.md` show as modified in `git status`. Those edits are from a concurrent session (an E6 judge mode decision entry and an Entire README sentence), not from E5; E5 touched only the files in the stage table.

### Components modified
| File | Component | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `src/lib/stormAtlas.ts` | summarize, shockedAtlasScenario, accountsInBand, entryBand | band counting, honest scenario wording |
| `src/lib/atlasPlot.ts` | buildAtlasPlot, jitterFor, binIndexFor | piecewise axis geometry, deterministic dots |
| `src/components/atlas/StormAtlas.tsx` | headline panel | headline, subline, five band cells |
| `src/components/atlas/AtlasStripPlot.tsx` | strip plot | 4,500 dots, silhouette, ticks, ring, drill click |
| `src/components/atlas/AtlasSection.tsx` | section shell | one useMemo derivation, loading/error notes, scroll to console |
| `src/components/atlas/atlas.css` | ax- styles | band mapping, panel, plot, cells |
| `src/components/weather/weather.css` | (trimmed) | wx-atlas block removed |
| `src/App.tsx` | shell | mounts `#atlas` above `#console` |
| `src/dashScan.test.ts` | content rule | registers E5 files and stylesheet |

### Verification Checklist
- [x] Design follows frontend-design skill principles (band vocabulary from the domain, headline as thesis, structure encodes the band edges)
- [x] Distinctive, not templated (piecewise band axis and hanging silhouette, not a generic bar chart)
- [x] Responsive down to mobile (auto-fit cells, clamped headline, wrapping subline, scaling SVG)
- [x] Visible keyboard focus (no new focusable controls; existing controls untouched)
- [x] Reduced motion respected (`scrollIntoView` swaps smooth for auto, zero animation in the section)
- [x] Accessibility (semantic list and figure, `role="img"` with headline as accessible name, glyph plus label plus count plus number redundant encoding, AA contrast on reused tokens)
- [x] No em dashes, double hyphens, or dash equivalents in new strings and comments (dashScan covers all new files and atlas.css)
- [x] Build succeeds (`npm run build`, typecheck, 479 tests, 160 pytest, engine verify PASS)
